title: Q-Learning
body:
The [[Reinforcement Learning]] algorithm this course teaches. Learn a table $Q(s, a)$ giving the
expected return from taking action $a$ in state $s$ and behaving well afterwards. Once you have
it, the policy is free: **in state $s$, take the action with the largest $Q$.**

## The update rule

After every step $(s, a, r, s')$:

$$Q(s,a) \leftarrow Q(s,a) + \alpha \Big[\, \underbrace{r + \gamma \max_{a'} Q(s', a')}_{\text{what we now think it is worth}} - \underbrace{Q(s,a)}_{\text{what we thought}} \,\Big]$$

The bracket is the **temporal difference error**: the gap between the old estimate and a fresh one
built from the reward just received plus the best value available from where you landed. Move the
old estimate a fraction $\alpha$ (the learning rate) toward the new one, and repeat.

**That is the whole algorithm.** Everything else is bookkeeping.

Read the pieces:

| Symbol | Is |
|---|---|
| $\alpha$ | learning rate: how much one experience moves the estimate |
| $\gamma$ | discount: how much the future counts |
| $r$ | the reward actually received |
| $\max_{a'} Q(s',a')$ | the value of the best thing available next, **assumed** rather than taken |

## Model-free and off-policy

**Model-free**: it never learns $P(s' \mid s, a)$. It does not know how the world works and does
not need to, because it learns values by being in the world rather than by reasoning about it.
That is the practical selling point, and the cost is sample count.

**Off-policy**: the $\max$ means it learns the value of the *optimal* policy while actually
behaving by some other one, typically $\epsilon$-greedy. So the agent can explore, take bad
actions deliberately, and still converge on the best strategy. SARSA is the on-policy sibling, and
it uses the action actually taken instead of the max, so it learns the value of the policy it is
following, exploration mistakes and all.

**It converges to the optimal $Q$** given enough visits to every state-action pair and a decaying
learning rate. That guarantee is genuine and is why the algorithm is taught, and the conditions
are exactly what fails in practice.

## Bootstrapping, and why it is strange

The update uses $Q(s')$, which is itself a guess. **The estimate is being improved using other
estimates**, with only $r$ as a grain of real information per step. It works because the real
rewards seep backwards through the table one step per visit: the state next to the goal learns
first, then its neighbours, then theirs.

That is also why it is slow, and the picture to hold: value propagates backwards from the reward,
one layer per pass.

## Where the table stops working

$Q$ has one entry per state-action pair. Chess has $10^{40}$ states and a robot arm has
continuous ones, so the table is impossible before the algorithm is.

The fix is to stop storing $Q$ and start **approximating** it, usually with a
[[Neural Network]] taking the state and returning a value per action. That is deep Q-learning, it
is how the Atari and Go results were built, and it is where this course's blocks 3 and 5 meet:
[[Gradient Descent]] minimising the temporal-difference error as a [[Loss Function]]. Not on the
syllabus, and it is the obvious next step from here.
